papers.core_contribution: This tutorial overview argues that deep generative models offer a more plausible model of cortical learning and provide a way to bridge the gap between emergentist connectionist models and structured Bayesian models of cognition.
papers.conclusion: The focus on deep architectures and generative learning represents a crucial step forward for connectionist modeling, offering a more plausible model of cortical learning and a way to bridge the gap between emergentist connectionist models and structured Bayesian models of cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Deep unsupervised learning in hierarchical generative models can discover structured and abstract representations of sensory data.
Linear read-out accuracy of internal representations improves with the depth of the network, indicating more explicit encoding of relevant features.
The approach can simulate human-like behavior in tasks such as numerosity comparison, producing psychometric functions that match human data.
future_direction: Incorporating convolutional layers to achieve translation invariance.
Learning temporal dynamics of data to anticipate events, as in predictive coding.
Unifying connectionist and Bayesian models of cognition within a deep generative network framework.
papers.abstract: Deep unsupervised learning in stochastic recurrent neural networks with many layers of hidden units is a recent breakthrough in neural computation research. These networks build a hierarchy of progressively more complex distributed representations of the sensory data by fitting a hierarchical generative model. In this article we discuss the theoretical foundations of this approach and we review key issues related to training, testing and analysis of deep networks for modeling language and cognitive processing. The classic letter and word perception problem of McClelland and Rumelhart (1981) is used as a tutorial example to illustrate how structured and abstract representations may emerge from deep generative learning. We argue that the focus on deep architectures and generative (rather than discriminative) learning represents a crucial step forward for the connectionist modeling enterprise, because it offers a more plausible model of cortical learning as well as a way to bridge the gap between emergentist connectionist models and structured Bayesian models of cognition.

papers.title: How Do Neural Sequence Models Generalize? Local and Global Context Cues\n for Out-of-Distribution Prediction
papers.research_question: How do neural sequence models generalize in out-of-distribution contexts when local and global context cues conflict?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models generalize in out-of-distribution contexts by interpolating between local and global context cues, and this interpolation can be controlled by noise-based regularization.
papers.conclusion: Neural sequence models' behavior in out-of-distribution contexts can be predicted and is approximated by interpolation of local and global cues, and noise can control this, suggesting avenues for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Neural LMs' out-of-distribution behavior is well approximated by either local or global context models, and best by a log-linear interpolation.
The preference for local vs. global generalization varies across languages (local works better for English and regular languages, global for Finnish and Chinese).
Noise during training can control the interpolation: input noise encourages global generalization, while history noise encourages local generalization.
A theoretical proposition shows that interpolation behavior arises in log-linear models with separate local and global features.
papers.limitation: The theoretical result relies on a feature function that may not realistically represent deep network features, involves strong assumptions, and becomes vacuous for certain parameter values.
future_direction: Explaining data-dependent aspects of the local-global trade-off, especially cross-linguistic differences.
Determining whether architectural improvements can more effectively target specific kinds of structured generalization.
papers.abstract:
After a neural sequence model encounters an unexpected token, can its
behavior be predicted? We show that RNN and transformer language models exhibit
structured, consistent generalization in out-of-distribution contexts. We begin
by introducing two idealized models of generalization in next-word prediction:
a local context model in which generalization is consistent with the last word
observed, and a global context model in which generalization is consistent with
the global structure of the input. In experiments in English, Finnish,
Mandarin, and random regular languages, we demonstrate that neural language
models interpolate between these two forms of generalization: their predictions
are well-approximated by a log-linear combination of local and global
predictive distributions. We then show that, in some languages, noise mediates
the two forms of generalization: noise applied to input tokens encourages
global generalization, while noise in history representations encourages local
generalization. Finally, we offer a preliminary theoretical explanation of
these results by proving that the observed interpolation behavior is expected
in log-linear models with a particular feature correlation structure. These
results help explain the effectiveness of two popular regularization schemes
and show that aspects of sequence model generalization can be understood and
controlled.

papers.title: Measuring In-Context Computation Complexity via Hidden State Prediction
papers.research_question: How can we measure the complexity or 'interestingness' of in-context computation performed by neural sequence models, given that next token prediction loss is a poor indicator?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a new metric, PHi loss, which measures the unpredictability of a model's own hidden states, and shows it correlates with the complexity and 'interestingness' of in-context computation, outperforming next token prediction loss.
papers.conclusion: The proposed PHi loss is a principled and effective metric for quantifying the complexity of in-context computation, offering a tool to detect when models are performing 'interesting' internal calculations.
papers.key_findings:
PHi loss is high for tasks requiring non-trivial in-context computation (e.g., in-context language learning, code, literature) and low for trivial or memorized tasks.
For in-context learning of formal languages, PHi loss predicts the description length (complexity) of the language beyond next token loss.
For mathematical reasoning, PHi loss is predictive of problem hardness and the correctness of model-generated step-by-step solutions.
When an LLM generates multiple rationales for a math problem, selecting the one with higher PHi loss significantly increases the chance of choosing the correct answer.
PHi loss provides a more meaningful indicator of computational complexity than next token loss, which fails to distinguish interesting from boring tasks.
papers.limitation:
The precise connection between PHi loss and formal concepts like sophistication remains an open question.
Copying or redundancy in sequences can lead to high PHi loss without constituting true 'interestingness'.
Hidden states require many bits to encode due to their high dimensionality, suggesting room for more efficient bottlenecks.
future_direction: Addressing the conceptual challenge of copying/redundancy in relation to interestingness.
Exploring alternative forms of information bottlenecks, such as quantized autoencoders.
Further theoretical investigation into the connection between PHi loss and formal measures of complexity.
papers.abstract: Detecting when a neural sequence model does "interesting" computation is an open problem. The next token prediction loss is a poor indicator: Low loss can stem from trivially predictable sequences that are uninteresting, while high loss may reflect unpredictable but also irrelevant information that can be ignored by the model. We propose a better metric: measuring the model's ability to predict its own future hidden states. We show empirically that this metric -- in contrast to the next token prediction loss -- correlates with the intuitive interestingness of the task. To measure predictability, we introduce the architecture-agnostic "prediction of hidden states" (PHi) layer that serves as an information bottleneck on the main pathway of the network (e.g., the residual stream in Transformers). We propose a novel learned predictive prior that enables us to measure the novel information gained in each computation step, which serves as our metric. We show empirically that our metric predicts the description length of formal languages learned in-context, the complexity of mathematical reasoning problems, and the correctness of self-generated reasoning chains.

papers.title: Language Models are Symbolic Learners in Arithmetic
papers.research_question: Do language models learn to truly compute arithmetic operations, or do they merely master superficial pattern matching?
papers.core_contribution: Language models act as greedy symbolic learners in arithmetic, learning a hierarchy of simple symbolic shortcuts rather than the underlying algorithm, as evidenced by a U-shaped accuracy pattern that aligns with subgroup quality.
papers.conclusion: Language models master arithmetic not by learning algorithms but by learning a hierarchy of simple symbolic shortcuts, acting as greedy symbolic learners.
papers.key_findings:
LMs show a U-shaped accuracy pattern in multi-digit multiplication, with high accuracy at the first and last digits and low accuracy in the middle.
The U-shape aligns with subgroup quality: simple shortcuts (few input tokens) exist for edge digits but not for middle digits.
LMs learn by first exploiting low-token, high-quality subgroups and gradually incorporating more tokens.
Subgroup entropy correlates with task difficulty and can be used for error estimation.
In CoT, the reasoning path with the lowest total subgroup entropy yields the best performance.
papers.limitation: Subgroup quality is computationally expensive for long sequences and not easily comparable across tasks.
future_direction: Investigate subgroup entropy's error estimation capabilities across tasks.
papers.abstract: The prevailing question in LM performing arithmetic is whether these models learn to truly compute or if they simply master superficial pattern matching. In this paper, we argues for the latter, presenting evidence that LMs act as greedy symbolic learners, prioritizing the simplest possible shortcuts to fit the stats of dataset to solve arithmetic tasks. To investigate this, we introduce subgroup induction, a practical framework adapted from Solomonoff Induction (SI), one of the most powerful universal predictors. Our framework analyzes arithmetic problems by breaking them down into subgroups-minimal mappings between a few input digits and a single output digit. Our primary metric, subgroup quality, measures the viability of these shortcuts. Experiments reveal a distinct U-shaped accuracy pattern in multi-digit multiplication: LMs quickly master the first and last output digits while struggling with those in the middle. We demonstrate this U-shape is not coincidental; it perfectly mirrors the quality of the simplest possible subgroups, those requiring the fewest input tokens. This alignment suggests a core learning mechanism: LMs first learn easy, low-token shortcuts and only incorporate more complex, multi-token patterns as training progresses. They do not learn the algorithm of multiplication but rather a hierarchy of increasingly complex symbol-to-symbol mappings. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the path to arithmetic mastery for LMs is not paved with algorithms, but with a cascade of simple, hierarchically-learned symbolic shortcuts.

papers.title: Structured Semantic Knowledge Can Emerge Automatically from Predicting Word Sequences in Child-Directed Speech
papers.research_question: Can neural networks trained to predict word sequences in child-directed speech acquire abstract and structured semantic knowledge? Do the acquired semantic structures reflect those of children, and how do different architectures compare?
papers.core_contribution: Recurrent neural networks trained to predict word sequences in child-directed speech can learn abstract and structured semantic knowledge, including categorical and hierarchical organization, supporting distributional learning as a mechanism for semantic development.
papers.conclusion: Structured semantic knowledge can emerge automatically from learning statistical regularities in child-directed speech, supporting a neural network model of statistical learning for semantic development.
papers.key_findings:
Learned internal representations encode abstract grammatical and semantic features useful for prediction.
Similarity structure of representations shows emergent categorical and hierarchical organization.
LSTM and SRN learn similar representations, but LSTM achieves higher quantitative performance.
Skip-gram performs similarly to LSTM but represents words more thematically than taxonomically.
Models' semantic spaces are consistent across random initializations and qualitatively similar to human semantic organization.
papers.limitation:
Models only use linguistic input and lack grounded, embodied world knowledge.
Input is limited to a subset of child-directed speech (CHILDES corpus).
Sequence prediction may overfit to language statistics at the expense of semantic classification.
Cognitive plausibility of some optimizations (e.g., in Skip-gram) is questionable.
future_direction: Extend models to include auditory and visual input for grounded learning.
Further experimental validation of model predictions against human data.
Quantify the extent of hierarchical representations in models.
papers.abstract: Previous research has suggested that distributional learning mechanisms may contribute to the acquisition of semantic knowledge. However, distributional learning mechanisms, statistical learning, and contemporary "deep learning" approaches have been criticized for being incapable of learning the kind of abstract and structured knowledge that many think is required for acquisition of semantic knowledge. In this paper, we show that recurrent neural networks, trained on noisy naturalistic speech to children, do in fact learn what appears to be abstract and structured knowledge. We trained two types of recurrent neural networks (Simple Recurrent Network, and Long Short-Term Memory) to predict word sequences in a 5-million-word corpus of speech directed to children ages 0-3 years old, and assessed what semantic knowledge they acquired. We found that learned internal representations are encoding various abstract grammatical and semantic features that are useful for predicting word sequences. Assessing the organization of semantic knowledge in terms of the similarity structure, we found evidence of emergent categorical and hierarchical structure in both models. We found that the Long Short-term Memory (LSTM) and SRN are both learning very similar kinds of representations, but the LSTM achieved higher levels of performance on a quantitative evaluation. We also trained a non-recurrent neural network, Skip-gram, on the same input to compare our results to the state-of-the-art in machine learning. We found that Skip-gram achieves relatively similar performance to the LSTM, but is representing words more in terms of thematic compared to taxonomic relations, and we provide reasons why this might be the case. Our findings show that a learning system that derives abstract, distributed representations for the purpose of predicting sequential dependencies in naturalistic language may provide insight into emergence of many properties of the developing semantic system.

papers.title: Visualisation and 'Diagnostic Classifiers' Reveal how Recurrent and Recursive Neural Networks Process Hierarchical Structure (Extended Abstract)
papers.research_question: How do recurrent neural networks learn and process languages with hierarchical, compositional semantics?
papers.core_contribution: Diagnostic classifiers reveal that gated recurrent neural networks follow a cumulative strategy when processing hierarchical arithmetic expressions, demonstrating the method's utility for interpreting neural network internals.
papers.conclusion: GRUs successfully process hierarchical structure by approximating a cumulative strategy, and diagnostic classifiers are an effective tool for analyzing neural network internal dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
GRUs can learn to compute the meaning of arithmetic expressions and generalize to longer expressions, while SRNs cannot.
Diagnostic classification shows that GRUs implement a strategy similar to the cumulative strategy, not the recursive strategy.
The method provides quantitative insights into network dynamics, overcoming limitations of visualization-based approaches.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate how recurrent neural networks can learn and process languages with hierarchical, compositional semantics. To this end, we define the artificial task of processing nested arithmetic expressions, and study whether different types of neural networks can learn to compute their meaning. We find that simple recurrent networks cannot find a generalising solution to this task, but gated recurrent neural networks perform surprisingly well: networks learn to predict the outcome of the arithmetic expressions with high accuracy, although performance deteriorates somewhat with increasing length. We test multiple hypotheses on the information that is encoded and processed by the networks using a method called diagnostic classification. In this method, simple neural classifiers are used to test sequences of predictions about features of the hidden state representations at each time step. Our results indicate that the networks follow a strategy similar to our hypothesised ‘cumulative strategy’, which explains the high accuracy of the network on novel expressions, the generalisation to longer expressions than seen in training, and the mild deterioration with increasing length. This, in turn, shows that diagnostic classifiers can be a useful technique for opening up the black box of neural networks.

papers.title: Visualisation and 'Diagnostic Classifiers' Reveal How Recurrent and Recursive Neural Networks Process Hierarchical Structure
papers.research_question: How do neural networks learn and process languages with hierarchical, compositional semantics, specifically whether they can compute the meaning of nested arithmetic expressions and how they do so.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces diagnostic classifiers as a method to analyze internal representations of recurrent neural networks and shows that GRUs follow a cumulative strategy for processing hierarchical arithmetic expressions.
papers.conclusion: Diagnostic classifiers can open the black box of neural networks and reveal the strategies they use, with GRUs approximating a cumulative strategy for processing hierarchical structure.
papers.key_findings:
TreeRNNs learn a recursive solution to compute arithmetic expressions and generalize to longer expressions.
GRUs can learn to compute arithmetic expressions and generalize, but performance deteriorates with length.
Diagnostic classifiers reveal that GRUs follow a strategy similar to a cumulative strategy, not a recursive strategy.
The method of diagnostic classifiers is proposed as a scalable way to analyze high-dimensional RNNs.
Visualization techniques like project-sum-squash provide insight into the TreeRNN's composition function.
papers.limitation:
Diagnostic classifiers for gates may require more complex architectures to handle non-linearities.
The analysis is on an idealized task and has not been applied to deeper networks and real-world tasks.
The network's strategy deviates from the perfect cumulative strategy, especially for right-branching expressions.
future_direction: Using diagnostic classifiers for gates with non-linear architectures.
Applying diagnostic classification to higher-dimensional networks and real-world tasks like language modeling and machine translation.
Further research into the reasons for the mismatch between the network's strategy and the cumulative strategy for right-branching expressions.
papers.abstract: We investigate how neural networks can learn and process languages with hierarchical, compositional semantics. To this end, we define the artificial task of processing nested arithmetic expressions, and study whether different types of neural networks can learn to compute their meaning. We find that recursive neural networks can implement a generalising solution to this problem, and we visualise this solution by breaking it up in three steps: project, sum and squash. As a next step, we investigate recurrent neural networks, and show that a gated recurrent unit, that processes its input incrementally, also performs very well on this task: the network learns to predict the outcome of the arithmetic expressions with high accuracy, although performance deteriorates somewhat with increasing length. To develop an understanding of what the recurrent network encodes, visualisation techniques alone do not suffice. Therefore, we develop an approach where we formulate and test multiple hypotheses on the information encoded and processed by the network. For each hypothesis, we derive predictions about features of the hidden state representations at each time step, and train 'diagnostic classifiers' to test those predictions. Our results indicate that the networks follow a strategy similar to our hypothesised 'cumulative strategy', which explains the high accuracy of the network on novel expressions, the generalisation to longer expressions than seen in training, and the mild deterioration with increasing length. This in turn shows that diagnostic classifiers can be a useful technique for opening up the black box of neural networks. We argue that diagnostic classification, unlike most visualisation techniques, does scale up from small networks in a toy domain, to larger and deeper recurrent networks dealing with real-life data, and may therefore contribute to a better understanding of the internal dynamics of current state-of-the-art models in natural language processing.

papers.title: Arithmetic with Language Models: from Memorization to Computation
papers.research_question: How does a language model perform arithmetic computations, and does it work as an Encoding-Regression-Decoding machine?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes and provides evidence for the Encoding-Regression-Decoding (ERD) hypothesis, where language models perform arithmetic by encoding tokens to values, performing regression in value space, and decoding back to tokens.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the LM solves arithmetic tasks via a regression in value space after encoding and before decoding, and that this ERD hypothesis is supported by their experiments.
papers.key_findings:
The LM can learn binary addition and multiplication from scratch and generalize well, indicating that memorization is not necessary.
Generalization is harder when a contiguous region in value space is excluded from training, supporting the ERD hypothesis.
Correlation analysis of internal embeddings shows that in the decoder, early and late layers correlate with token-level distances, while middle layers correlate with value-level distances, suggesting encoding and decoding happen in early/late layers and regression in middle layers.
Amnesic probing shows that removing value information from middle layer embeddings severely degrades performance, indicating that value information is causally important.
Ablation study shows that positional embedding and attention layers are necessary for the task, while the encoder can be simplified.
future_direction: Further investigate the generalization capabilities of LMs in arithmetic tasks with respect to the composition of the training and test sets.
Design simplified experiments/setups for tasks that cannot be easily mapped to regression problems such as chain of reasoning and logic deductions.
papers.abstract: A better understanding of the emergent computation and problem-solving capabilities of recent large language models is of paramount importance to further improve them and broaden their applicability. This work investigates how a language model, trained to predict the next token, can perform arithmetic computations generalizing beyond training data. Binary addition and multiplication constitute a good testbed for this purpose, since they require a very small vocabulary and exhibit relevant input/output discontinuities making smooth input interpolation ineffective for novel data. We successfully trained a light language model to learn these tasks and ran a number of experiments to investigate the extrapolation capabilities and internal information processing. Our findings support the hypothesis that the language model works as an Encoding-Regression-Decoding machine where the computation takes place in the value space once the input token representation is mapped to an appropriate internal representation.

papers.title: I Predict Therefore I Am: Is Next Token Prediction Enough to Learn Human-Interpretable Concepts from Data?
papers.research_question: Is next-token prediction sufficient for large language models to learn human-interpretable concepts from data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes that LLM representations learned via next-token prediction are approximately a linear transformation of the log-posterior of latent human-interpretable concepts, providing a theoretical foundation for the linear representation hypothesis and motivating a principled evaluation method for sparse autoencoders.
papers.conclusion: Next-token prediction enables LLMs to learn human-interpretable concepts, and the linear identifiability result offers a unified perspective on the linear representation hypothesis and a principled approach for evaluating concept disentanglement methods like sparse autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
Under mild conditions, LLM representations are approximately a linear transformation of the log-posterior of latent concepts.
This linear property provides a unified explanation for empirical phenomena like concepts as directions and linear probing.
The linear property motivates a principled evaluation method for sparse autoencoders using linear probes.
Structured SAEs, which incorporate low-rank regularization, improve concept disentanglement compared to standard SAEs.
Empirical validation on simulation data and multiple LLM families (Pythia, Llama, DeepSeek) supports the theoretical results.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis relies on assumptions such as the diversity condition and approximate invertibility, which may not hold in all scenarios.
The evaluation of sparse autoencoders depends on the quality of linear probes, which may be noisy.
future_direction: Rethinking invertibility assumptions in causal representation learning.
Embedding causal reasoning in LLMs through linear unmixing.
papers.abstract: The remarkable achievements of large language models (LLMs) have led many to conclude that they exhibit a form of intelligence. This is as opposed to explanations of their capabilities based on their ability to perform relatively simple manipulations of vast volumes of data. To illuminate the distinction between these explanations, we introduce a novel generative model that generates tokens on the basis of human-interpretable concepts represented as latent discrete variables. Under mild conditions, even when the mapping from the latent space to the observed space is non-invertible, we establish an identifiability result, i.e., the representations learned by LLMs through next-token prediction can be approximately modeled as the logarithm of the posterior probabilities of these latent discrete concepts given input context, up to an invertible linear transformation. This theoretical finding not only provides evidence that LLMs capture underlying generative factors, but also provide a unified prospective for understanding of the linear representation hypothesis. Taking this a step further, our finding motivates a reliable evaluation of sparse autoencoders by treating the performance of supervised concept extractors as an upper bound. Pushing this idea even further, it inspires a structural variant that enforces dependence among latent concepts in addition to promoting sparsity. Empirically, we validate our theoretical results through evaluations on both simulation data and the Pythia, Llama, and DeepSeek model families, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our structured sparse autoencoder.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 2.1, Grade-School Math and the Hidden Reasoning Process
papers.research_question: How do language models solve grade-school math problems? Do they memorize templates or learn reasoning skills? What is the hidden reasoning process and what causes mistakes?
papers.core_contribution: Language models trained on synthetic grade-school math problems can learn reasoning skills, generalize to longer reasoning lengths, and internally compute unnecessary dependencies, indicating learning beyond the training objective.
papers.conclusion: Language models can learn genuine reasoning skills from synthetic data, and depth is more important than width for reasoning ability.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve high accuracy and generalize to longer reasoning lengths than seen during training.
Models generate shortest solutions, avoiding unnecessary computations, suggesting planning.
Probing reveals the model preprocesses necessary parameters before generation.
Models learn to compute all-pair dependencies, a skill not required by the training data.
Mistakes can be explained by probing internal states and are sometimes predictable.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not directly apply to foundation models like GPT-4 or more challenging mathematical reasoning tasks.
Uses synthetic data with modulo arithmetic, which may not reflect real-world math problems.
future_direction: Physics of Language Models: Part 2.2, How to Learn From Mistakes on Grade-School Math Problems
papers.abstract: Recent advances in language models have demonstrated their capability to solve mathematical reasoning problems, achieving near-perfect accuracy on grade-school level math benchmarks like GSM8K. In this paper, we formally study how language models solve these problems. We design a series of controlled experiments to address several fundamental questions: (1) Can language models truly develop reasoning skills, or do they simply memorize templates? (2) What is the model's hidden (mental) reasoning process? (3) Do models solve math questions using skills similar to or different from humans? (4) Do models trained on GSM8K-like datasets develop reasoning skills beyond those necessary for solving GSM8K problems? (5) What mental process causes models to make reasoning mistakes? (6) How large or deep must a model be to effectively solve GSM8K-level math questions? Our study uncovers many hidden mechanisms by which language models solve mathematical questions, providing insights that extend beyond current understandings of LLMs.

papers.title: Neural Language Models as Psycholinguistic Subjects: Representations of Syntactic State
papers.research_question: To what extent do neural network language models reflect incremental representations of syntactic state?
papers.core_contribution: Large LSTMs trained on large datasets can represent syntactic state comparably to an explicitly syntactic model (RNNG), and data size is crucial for learning fine-grained lexical cues to syntactic structure.
papers.conclusion: All models show basic incremental syntactic state representation, but capturing fine-grained lexical cues requires large amounts of data, while coarse-grained structure can be learned with either syntactic supervision or large data.
papers.key_findings:
All tested models show basic evidence of incremental syntactic state representation (e.g., subordinate clause licensing).
Only the large LSTMs (GRNN, JRNN) and the RNNG fully capture the proper behavior of subordinate clauses (no-matrix penalty).
All models show NP/Z garden path effects, but only large LSTMs are sensitive to verb transitivity as a cue.
All models show MV/RR garden path effects, but only large LSTMs and the RNNG are sensitive to verb morphology as a cue.
The representation of syntactic state degrades with increasing intervening material in some models (GRNN and TinyLSTM).
future_direction: Using psycholinguistic methodology as a basis for more systematic tests of the linguistic competence of NLP systems.
papers.abstract: We deploy the methods of controlled psycholinguistic experimentation to shed light on the extent to which the behavior of neural network language models reflects incremental representations of syntactic state. To do so, we examine model behavior on artificial sentences containing a variety of syntactically complex structures. We test four models: two publicly available LSTM sequence models of English (Jozefowicz et al., 2016; Gulordava et al., 2018) trained on large datasets; an RNNG (Dyer et al., 2016) trained on a small, parsed dataset; and an LSTM trained on the same small corpus as the RNNG. We find evidence that the LSTMs trained on large datasets represent syntactic state over large spans of text in a way that is comparable to the RNNG, while the LSTM trained on the small dataset does not or does so only weakly.

papers.title: Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing
papers.research_question: How are high-level human-interpretable features represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs, and how does the sparsity of these representations vary with model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sparse probing to localize individual neurons representing features in LLMs, revealing that early layers use superposition (sparse combinations of polysemantic neurons), middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons for higher-level features, and model scale increases representational sparsity with varied dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Sparse probing is a powerful tool for understanding feature representation in LLMs, revealing superposition in early layers and monosemantic neurons in middle layers, with scaling effects on sparsity, and opens many directions for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers represent many features in superposition via sparse linear combinations of polysemantic neurons.
Middle layers contain seemingly dedicated (monosemantic) neurons for higher-level contextual features like language or code.
Increasing model scale generally increases representational sparsity, but different features exhibit distinct scaling dynamics.
Sparse probing is an effective method for locating interpretable neurons, even when they are in superposition.
There is a tremendous amount of interpretable structure within the neurons of LLMs, accessible through careful probing and analysis.
papers.limitation:
Interpretation of neurons can be misleading due to 'interpretability illusions' from only examining maximum activating examples.
Conclusive statements about monosemanticity remain methodologically out of reach.
future_direction: Apply sparse probing to other model families and architectures.
Study the dynamics of feature representation during training, not just in final models.
Extend sparse probing to multimodal models and other modalities.
papers.abstract: Despite rapid adoption and deployment of large language models (LLMs), the internal computations of these models remain opaque and poorly understood. In this work, we seek to understand how high-level human-interpretable features are represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs. We train $k$-sparse linear classifiers (probes) on these internal activations to predict the presence of features in the input; by varying the value of $k$ we study the sparsity of learned representations and how this varies with model scale. With $k=1$, we localize individual neurons which are highly relevant for a particular feature, and perform a number of case studies to illustrate general properties of LLMs. In particular, we show that early layers make use of sparse combinations of neurons to represent many features in superposition, that middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons to represent higher-level contextual features, and that increasing scale causes representational sparsity to increase on average, but there are multiple types of scaling dynamics. In all, we probe for over 100 unique features comprising 10 different categories in 7 different models spanning 70 million to 6.9 billion parameters.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: Algorithmic Capabilities of Random Transformers
papers.research_question: To what extent do the circuits that implement interpretable procedures in transformers depend on the supervisory signal provided during training, and to what extent are they attributable to behavior already present in models at initialization?
papers.core_contribution: Randomly initialized transformers, with only their embedding and unembedding layers trained, can successfully perform a range of algorithmic and language modeling tasks, indicating that these capabilities are inherent to the transformer architecture and accessible at initialization via appropriate input encodings.
papers.conclusion: Transformer models possess inherent algorithmic capabilities at initialization that can be accessed by training only their embedding layers, suggesting that some interpretable circuits are present even before training and highlighting the strong inductive bias of the architecture.
papers.key_findings:
Random transformers with embedding-only training achieve perfect accuracy on modular addition, needle-in-a-haystack, decimal addition, and parenthesis balancing tasks.
They outperform fully trained LSTMs on some algorithmic tasks and exhibit interpretable attention patterns similar to induction heads.
Learned embeddings for tasks like modular addition form structured low-dimensional representations (e.g., circles).
Random transformers can memorize arbitrary associations but with lower parameter efficiency than fully trained transformers.
They can generate grammatical natural language text, though with lower coherence and perplexity than fully trained models.
papers.limitation:
The space of architectural decisions (model size, attention mechanisms, normalization, tokenization) is large, and the described trends may change with different parameterizations.
The analysis focuses on standard transformers and does not address whether trends hold in other architectures like linear attention or state-space models.
The subspace analysis uses linear PCA and may not capture non-linear subspaces or latent semantics.
future_direction: Investigate how learned feature codebooks and automated neuron labeling procedures behave when applied to random transformers.
Closer study of untrained models as a source of insight for improving neural model architectures.
papers.abstract: Trained transformer models have been found to implement interpretable procedures for tasks like arithmetic and associative recall, but little is understood about how the circuits that implement these procedures originate during training. To what extent do they depend on the supervisory signal provided to models, and to what extent are they attributable to behavior already present in models at the beginning of training? To investigate these questions, we investigate what functions can be learned by randomly initialized transformers in which only the embedding layers are optimized, so that the only input--output mappings learnable from data are those already implemented (up to a choice of encoding scheme) by the randomly initialized model. We find that these random transformers can perform a wide range of meaningful algorithmic tasks, including modular arithmetic, in-weights and in-context associative recall, decimal addition, parenthesis balancing, and even some aspects of natural language text generation. Our results indicate that some algorithmic capabilities are present in transformers (and accessible via appropriately structured inputs) even before these models are trained. Code is available at https://github.com/fjzzq2002/random_transformers.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: Sequential Enumeration in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can large language models robustly and systematically deploy counting procedures for sequential enumeration tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can perform sequential enumeration when explicitly instructed to count, but fail to do so spontaneously, indicating a lack of robust and systematic counting abilities.
papers.conclusion: LLMs cannot yet robustly and systematically deploy counting procedures, highlighting a persistent gap between neural and symbolic approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Proprietary models achieve high accuracy in production tasks when explicitly asked to count.
Accuracy drops significantly in naming tasks and when counting is not explicitly instructed.
Models do not spontaneously engage in counting.
Internal dynamics show different computational strategies for explicit vs. mental counting.
Model size improves performance gradually but not emergently.
papers.limitation: LLMs do not spontaneously engage in counting when not explicitly instructed.
papers.abstract: Reliably counting and generating sequences of items remain a significant challenge for neural networks, including Large Language Models (LLMs). Indeed, although this capability is readily handled by rule-based symbolic systems based on serial computation, learning to systematically deploy counting procedures is difficult for neural models, which should acquire these skills through learning. Previous research has demonstrated that recurrent architectures can only approximately track and enumerate sequences of events, and it remains unclear whether modern deep learning systems, including LLMs, can deploy systematic counting procedures over sequences of discrete symbols. This paper aims to fill this gap by investigating the sequential enumeration abilities of five state-of-the-art LLMs, including proprietary, open-source, and reasoning models. We probe LLMs in sequential naming and production tasks involving lists of letters and words, adopting a variety of prompting instructions to explore the role of chain-of-thought in the spontaneous emerging of counting strategies. We also evaluate open-source models with the same architecture but increasing size to see whether the mastering of counting principles follows scaling laws, and we analyze the embedding dynamics during sequential enumeration to investigate the emergent encoding of numerosity. We find that some LLMs are indeed capable of deploying counting procedures when explicitly prompted to do so, but none of them spontaneously engage in counting when simply asked to enumerate the number of items in a sequence. Our results suggest that, despite their impressive emergent abilities, LLMs cannot yet robustly and systematically deploy counting procedures, highlighting a persistent gap between neural and symbolic approaches to compositional generalization.

papers.title: A Sentence is Worth a Thousand Pictures: Can Large Language Models Understand Hum4n L4ngu4ge and the W0rld behind W0rds?
papers.research_question: Are humans and LLMs equally accurate in decoding leetspeak, and can they equally explain the substitutions?
papers.core_contribution: Humans outperform LLMs in decoding leetspeak, demonstrating that LLMs lack top-down processing and grounded cognition, which are essential for human-like language understanding.
papers.conclusion: LLMs do not possess human-like linguistic competence; superficial similarity in output does not imply system equivalence, and models lack grounded cognition and top-down processing.
papers.key_findings:
Humans achieve near-ceiling accuracy in decoding leetspeak, while LLMs perform worse.
ChatGPT-4o is the best-performing model but still below humans, especially with more substitutions.
LLMs show an accuracy-reasoning mismatch, often decoding correctly but failing to explain substitutions.
Model errors are qualitatively different from human errors, indicating a lack of common sense and real-world grounding.
Performance differences suggest LLMs rely on form-based associations rather than meaning.
future_direction: Future language models may need to take an entirely different approach, beginning with deeper semantics and cognitive models of the world.
A closer examination of how LLM outputs align with subtle syntactic, acceptability judgments in humans.
Combining deep learning with models of symbolic cognition.
papers.abstract: Modern Artificial Intelligence applications show great potential for language-related tasks that rely on next-word prediction. The current generation of Large Language Models (LLMs) have been linked to claims about human-like linguistic performance and their applications are hailed both as a step towards artificial general intelligence and as a major advance in understanding the cognitive, and even neural basis of human language. To assess these claims, first we analyze the contribution of LLMs as theoretically informative representations of a target cognitive system vs. atheoretical mechanistic tools. Second, we evaluate the models' ability to see the bigger picture, through top-down feedback from higher levels of processing, which requires grounding in previous expectations and past world experience. We hypothesize that since models lack grounded cognition, they cannot take advantage of these features and instead solely rely on fixed associations between represented words and word vectors. To assess this, we designed and ran a novel 'leet task' (l33t t4sk), which requires decoding sentences in which letters are systematically replaced by numbers. The results suggest that humans excel in this task whereas models struggle, confirming our hypothesis. We interpret the results by identifying the key abilities that are still missing from the current state of development of these models, which require solutions that go beyond increased system scaling.

papers.title: Superscopes: Amplifying Internal Feature Representations for Language Model Interpretation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret internal representations (like MLP outputs and hidden states) in language models that are not interpretable with existing self-interpretation methods, by amplifying weak features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Superscopes, a method that amplifies weak features in internal representations (MLP outputs and hidden states) to enable their interpretation via self-interpretation methods like Patchscopes, without requiring additional training.
papers.conclusion: Superscopes extends Patchscopes by amplifying internal representations, enabling interpretation of previously uninterpretable MLP outputs and hidden states, and draws a parallel to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models.
papers.key_findings:
Amplifying MLP outputs reveals meaningful interpretations that are not accessible with standard Patchscopes.
Amplifying hidden states can reveal interpretations in layers before contextualization occurs.
The amplification technique is analogous to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models, as both amplify directional shifts.
The Superscopes framework can automatically identify optimal amplification factors for interpretation.
The method demonstrates that weak features in internal representations can be amplified to reveal semantic content.
papers.limitation:
The method does not currently handle attention outputs, which may have a denser superposition of features.
The method for selecting the optimal amplifier may not be fully effective and could be improved.
future_direction: Extracting meaning from attention outputs.
Developing more effective approaches for selecting the optimal amplifier.
Exploring alternative ways to amplify meaning within Superscopes, such as using a different base vector for patching.
papers.abstract: Understanding and interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains an open challenge. Patchscopes introduced a method for probing internal activations by patching them into new prompts, prompting models to self-explain their hidden representations. We introduce Superscopes, a technique that systematically amplifies superposed features in MLP outputs (multilayer perceptron) and hidden states before patching them into new contexts. Inspired by the "features as directions" perspective and the Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) approach from diffusion models, Superscopes amplifies weak but meaningful features, enabling the interpretation of internal representations that previous methods failed to explain-all without requiring additional training. This approach provides new insights into how LLMs build context and represent complex concepts, further advancing mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number
papers.research_question: How does BERT encode grammatical number, and does it actually use that encoding when solving the number agreement task?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a usage-based probing setup to find functional encodings, and shows that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number for number agreement, with separate encodings for nouns and verbs, and identifies transfer layers.
papers.conclusion: The usage-based probing method allows tracking how grammatical number is encoded and transferred in BERT, showing that interventions impact behavior and extractability, revealing orthogonal encodings for nouns and verbs, and indirect transfer through intermediate tokens.
papers.key_findings:
BERT relies on a linear functional encoding of grammatical number to solve the number agreement task.
BERT uses separate encodings of grammatical number for nouns and verbs.
Number information is transferred from noun to verb between layers 3 and 8.
The transfer occurs indirectly through intermediate tokens, not directly via attention.
The encoding found by diagnostic probes is actually used by the model (functional).
papers.limitation:
The dataset may not be fully representative of the number agreement task.
Amnesic probing may remove more information than necessary.
papers.abstract: A central quest of probing is to uncover how pre-trained models encode a linguistic property within their representations. An encoding, however, might be spurious-i.e., the model might not rely on it when making predictions. In this paper, we try to find an encoding that the model actually uses, introducing a usage-based probing setup. We first choose a behavioral task which cannot be solved without using the linguistic property. Then, we attempt to remove the property by intervening on the model's representations. We contend that, if an encoding is used by the model, its removal should harm the performance on the chosen behavioral task. As a case study, we focus on how BERT encodes grammatical number, and on how it uses this encoding to solve the number agreement task. Experimentally, we find that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number to produce the correct behavioral output. We also find that BERT uses a separate encoding of grammatical number for nouns and verbs. Finally, we identify in which layers information about grammatical number is transferred from a noun to its head verb.

papers.title: On Representational Dissociation of Language and Arithmetic in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What about the language-thought dissociation in large language models? Specifically, are language and arithmetic inputs encoded in separate regions in LLMs' internal representation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that language and arithmetic inputs are encoded in completely separated regions in LLMs' internal representation space, and that math word problems form a separate cluster, suggesting fine-grained modularity beyond a coarse language-arithmetic dissociation.
papers.conclusion: This study explores the representational dissociation between language and arithmetic stimuli in LLMs, setting a direction to bridge neuroscientific perspectives with LLM internal analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Language and arithmetic equations are encoded in completely separated regions across all layers of LLMs.
The separation is not due to token differences, as spelled-out equations are also separated from language inputs.
Math word problems (GSM8K) form a separate cluster from both language and arithmetic regions.
The arithmetic region activated with primitive stimuli is not used in more complex arithmetic-involved tasks.
There are numerous arithmetic regions for different task formats, indicating fine-grained modularity.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to geometrical properties of the representation space; causal analysis is needed to align with actual abilities.
The generality of findings could be enhanced with other methodologies, such as gradient descent, magnitude of neuron activations, or activation probability.
The topic should be addressed through different experimental designs, e.g., ablating language learning scenarios.
future_direction: Incorporate alternative approaches to identify language and arithmetic regions, such as gradient descent, magnitude of neuron activations, or activation probability.
Conduct causal analysis to test whether the observed geometrical dissociation aligns with actual abilities.
Contextualize the results with existing LM-brain alignment studies.
Address the learnability of specific abilities through different experimental designs, e.g., ablating language learning scenarios.
papers.abstract: The association between language and (non-linguistic) thinking ability in humans has long been debated, and recently, neuroscientific evidence of brain activity patterns has been considered. Such a scientific context naturally raises an interdisciplinary question -- what about such a language-thought dissociation in large language models (LLMs)? In this paper, as an initial foray, we explore this question by focusing on simple arithmetic skills (e.g., $1+2=$ ?) as a thinking ability and analyzing the geometry of their encoding in LLMs' representation space. Our experiments with linear classifiers and cluster separability tests demonstrate that simple arithmetic equations and general language input are encoded in completely separated regions in LLMs' internal representation space across all the layers, which is also supported with more controlled stimuli (e.g., spelled-out equations). These tentatively suggest that arithmetic reasoning is mapped into a distinct region from general language input, which is in line with the neuroscientific observations of human brain activations, while we also point out their somewhat cognitively implausible geometric properties.

papers.title: Addition in Four Movements: Mapping Layer-wise Information Trajectories in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct perform multi-digit addition through structured, algorithmic computation (e.g., digit-wise summation with carry propagation), or through non-algorithmic pattern extraction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a consistent four-stage, layer-wise ordering of information when LLMs perform multi-digit addition (formula structure, core computations, numerical abstractions, output alignment), supporting a hierarchical, computation-first account rather than rote pattern matching.
papers.conclusion: The sequential emergence of features supports a structured, computation-like process in LLMs for addition, rather than rote memorization, and the observed trajectory is robust across architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers (1) encode formula structure (operand/operator layout) while the gold next token is still far from top-1.
Mid layers (2) expose digit-wise sums and carry indicators.
Deeper layers (3) express result-level numerical abstractions that support near-perfect digit decoding from hidden states.
Near the output (4), representations align with final sequence generation, with the correct next token reliably ranked first.
The four-stage ordering is consistent across experiments and models (with minor depth shifts), with each signal family becoming linearly decodable with high accuracy (typically ≥95%).
papers.limitation:
Correlation vs. causation: linear probes and logit lens are correlational, not causal.
Task scope: only in-distribution, base-10 multi-digit addition under short prompts.
Model specificity: main analysis on LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, though other models show similar ordering but with varying layer indices.
future_direction: Causal interventions (e.g., activation patching, targeted ablations) to establish dependence on intermediate computations.
papers.abstract: Multi-digit addition is a clear probe of the computational power of large language models. To dissect the internal arithmetic processes in LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, we combine linear probing with logit-lens inspection. Inspired by the step-by-step manner in which humans perform addition, we propose and analyze a coherent four-stage trajectory in the forward pass:Formula-structure representations become linearly decodable first, while the answer token is still far down the candidate list.Core computational features then emerge prominently.At deeper activation layers, numerical abstractions of the result become clearer, enabling near-perfect detection and decoding of the individual digits in the sum.Near the output, the model organizes and generates the final content, with the correct token reliably occupying the top rank.This trajectory suggests a hierarchical process that favors internal computation over rote memorization. We release our code and data to facilitate reproducibility.

papers.title: Interpreting Arithmetic Mechanism in Large Language Models through Comparative Neuron Analysis
papers.research_question: How is arithmetic ability implemented in large language models, specifically the role of attention heads and FFN neurons, and what is the internal logic chain from input to prediction? Additionally, how does the LoRA fine-tuning method work?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Comparative Neuron Analysis (CNA) method to interpret arithmetic mechanisms in LLMs, identifying an internal logic chain of four stages, and applies it to understand LoRA and for model pruning and bias reduction.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies important attention heads and FFN neurons for arithmetic, proposes the CNA method to construct the internal logic chain, finds LoRA amplifies important FFN neurons, and applies CNA to model pruning and editing.
papers.key_findings:
Arithmetic ability is localized in a few attention heads (arithmetic heads), each specializing in distinct operations.
The internal logic chain from input to prediction consists of four stages: feature enhancing, feature transferring, feature predicting, and prediction enhancing.
LoRA enhances prediction probabilities by amplifying the coefficient scores of important FFN neurons related to the final prediction.
Model pruning retaining only 5% of deep FFN neurons identified by CNA maintains performance on arithmetic tasks.
Model editing by zeroing 18 FFN neurons identified by CNA reduces gender bias by 35.7%.
papers.limitation:
The case studies rely on projecting vectors in vocabulary space, which is empirically interpretable but lacks complete theoretical foundation.
There is a lack of standardization across various studies regarding attribution methods (e.g., different intervention methods).
A potential risk is that attackers can identify and edit important neurons to change model behavior maliciously.
future_direction: Further investigation of the multiplication heads which do not significantly impact accuracy.
Explorations on different datasets for gender bias reduction.
Distinguishing whether a model has been edited to prevent malicious use.

papers.title: Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language
papers.research_question: Do large language models have the ability to introspect about their internal linguistic knowledge, specifically grammatical knowledge and word prediction?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs do not exhibit introspection about their linguistic knowledge; their metalinguistic responses are not more aligned with their own internal probabilities than with those of similar models.
papers.conclusion: LLMs cannot introspect about their linguistic knowledge, and metalinguistic prompting should not be conflated with models' internal linguistic generalizations.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve high accuracy on grammaticality and word prediction tasks under both direct (probability-based) and metalinguistic (prompt-based) evaluation methods.
The consistency between direct and metalinguistic evaluations is low (Cohen’s κ around 0.25).
There is no evidence of introspection: within-model alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations is not higher than cross-model alignment when controlling for model similarity.
Model similarity (both feature-based and empirical) predicts the alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations, but there is no additional 'same model effect'.
Larger models tend to have better performance on metalinguistic prompts and their metalinguistic responses are more correlated with direct evaluations.
papers.limitation:
The study only tested open-source models; closed-source models might behave differently.
The null result might be due to the specific tasks and models; introspection might emerge in other settings.
papers.abstract: There has been recent interest in whether large language models (LLMs) can introspect about their own internal states. Such abilities would make LLMs more interpretable, and also validate the use of standard introspective methods in linguistics to evaluate grammatical knowledge in models (e.g., asking "Is this sentence grammatical?"). We systematically investigate emergent introspection across 21 open-source LLMs, in two domains where introspection is of theoretical interest: grammatical knowledge and word prediction. Crucially, in both domains, a model's internal linguistic knowledge can be theoretically grounded in direct measurements of string probability. We then evaluate whether models' responses to metalinguistic prompts faithfully reflect their internal knowledge. We propose a new measure of introspection: the degree to which a model's prompted responses predict its own string probabilities, beyond what would be predicted by another model with nearly identical internal knowledge. While both metalinguistic prompting and probability comparisons lead to high task accuracy, we do not find evidence that LLMs have privileged "self-access". By using general tasks, controlling for model similarity, and evaluating a wide range of open-source models, we show that LLMs cannot introspect, and add new evidence to the argument that prompted responses should not be conflated with models' linguistic generalizations.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Think-to-Talk or Talk-to-Think? When LLMs Come Up with an Answer in Multi-Hop Arithmetic Reasoning
papers.research_question: When during chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning do LLMs determine their final answer, and how causally dependent is the answer on the CoT explanation?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT generation, and the CoT explanations are faithful reflections of their internal computation, not post-hoc justifications.
papers.conclusion: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT, making CoT explanations faithful to the internal reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not determine the final answer before CoT begins; instead, they compute sub-answers during CoT generation.
Linear probes show that answers become linearly separable in hidden states only after corresponding reasoning steps in CoT.
Causal interventions show that the final answer depends causally on the CoT part, especially the latter steps, showing recency bias.
The model's internal reasoning follows a recency bias: each step causally depends on the previous step.
For distractors (unnecessary variables), the model does not encode them in a linearly separable form, indicating efficient internal mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The study uses synthetic arithmetic tasks, which may not generalize to natural language reasoning.
The cause of incorrect answers in some instances remains unclear.
future_direction: Investigate more complex and natural language reasoning tasks.
Detailed analysis of error cases and internal representations of digits.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the incremental, internal problem-solving process of language models (LMs) with arithmetic multi-hop reasoning as a case study. We specifically investigate when LMs internally resolve sub/whole problems through first reading the problem statements, generating reasoning chains, and achieving the final answer to mechanistically interpret LMs' multi-hop problem-solving process. Our experiments reveal a systematic incremental reasoning strategy underlying LMs. They have not derived an answer at the moment they first read the problem; instead, they obtain (sub)answers while generating the reasoning chain. Therefore, the generated reasoning chains can be regarded as faithful reflections of the model's internal computation.

papers.title: Benford's Curse: Tracing Digit Bias to Numerical Hallucination in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does the skewed digit distribution in LLMs' pretraining corpus (following Benford's Law) induce digit generation bias, leading to numerical hallucination?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that digit bias in pretraining data (following Benford's Law) is internalized by LLMs, primarily in later-layer FFN neurons, and causally contributes to numerical hallucinations; pruning these biased neurons can mitigate the bias.
papers.conclusion: Digit bias originating from pretraining corpus statistics is a fundamental cause of numerical hallucinations in LLMs, and targeted intervention on biased neurons offers a potential mitigation strategy.
papers.key_findings:
The digit distribution in the pretraining corpus (Olmo-mix-1124) strongly aligns with Benford's Law, favoring smaller leading digits.
LLMs consistently overgenerate smaller digits in numerical reasoning tasks, even when ground-truth digits are uniformly distributed.
The digit bias is primarily driven by a subset of highly digit-selective feed-forward network (FFN) neurons concentrated in the deeper layers of the model.
When the model generates an incorrect answer, the first erroneous digit shows an even stronger skew toward smaller values, following Benford's Law.
Pruning neurons most selective for digit '1' can partially correct erroneous outputs, providing causal evidence that digit bias contributes to numerical hallucination.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted on relatively small-scale decoder-only LLMs (7B–9B parameters); whether similar patterns persist in larger models or Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models remains an open question.
The neuron pruning strategy is coarse and may disrupt correct generations, limiting overall accuracy gains.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger models and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures.
Developing more fine-grained or adaptive debiasing methods beyond simple pruning.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit impressive performance on complex reasoning tasks, yet they frequently fail on basic numerical problems, producing incorrect outputs. Inspired by Benford's Law, a statistical pattern in which lower digits occur more frequently as leading digits, we hypothesize that the skewed digit distributions in web-collected corpora may be learned by LLMs during pretraining, leading to biased numerical generation. To investigate the hypothesis, we first examine whether digits frequencies in pretraining corpus (OLMo2) follows Benford's law. We then construct an evaluation benchmark in which the ground-truth digits are uniformly distributed within each of the seven numerical reasoning tasks. Our evaluation results demonstrate that leading open-source LLMs show a consistent pattern of digit bias that resembles Benford's law. Through logit-lens tracing and neuron-level dissection, we identify that this bias arises predominantly from a small subset of highly digit-selective feed-forward network (FFN) neurons in the deeper layers. Finally, we demonstrate that pruning these neurons mitigates imbalanced overgeneration and partially corrects erroneous outputs, providing causal evidence that fine-grained pretraining digit bias can propagate into model behavior. Our findings reveal a fundamental connection between corpus-level statistics and symbolic failure modes in LLMs, offering a new lens for diagnosing and mitigating hallucinations in numerical tasks.

papers.title: Structural Persistence in Language Models: Priming as a Window into Abstract Language Representations
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether modern neural language models exhibit structural priming, what factors influence the priming effect, and the nature of the structural representations they acquire.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer language models exhibit structural priming, indicating they encode abstract structural information, and that this priming is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, with evidence for hierarchical syntactic representations.
