SAE features enable effective diffusion-time interventions (steering) that often outperform single-pass LLM steering.
SAE feature dynamics provide a useful signal for analyzing and correlating with the performance of different DLM decoding-order strategies.
Base-trained SAEs transfer almost losslessly to instruction-tuned DLMs in shallow and middle layers, but not in the deepest layer, indicating tuning-specific changes in deep representations.
future_direction: As DLMs scale, we plan to extend SAEs to more DLMs to better understand and improve models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a standard tool for mechanistic interpretability in autoregressive large language models (LLMs), enabling researchers to extract sparse, human-interpretable features and intervene on model behavior. Recently, as diffusion language models (DLMs) have become an increasingly promising alternative to the autoregressive LLMs, it is essential to develop tailored mechanistic interpretability tools for this emerging class of models. In this work, we present DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for DLMs, and demonstrate that trained Top-K SAEs can faithfully extract interpretable features. Notably, we find that inserting SAEs affects DLMs differently than autoregressive LLMs: while SAE insertion in LLMs typically incurs a loss penalty, in DLMs it can reduce cross-entropy loss when applied to early layers, a phenomenon absent or markedly weaker in LLMs. Additionally, SAE features in DLMs enable more effective diffusion-time interventions, often outperforming LLM steering. Moreover, we pioneer certain new SAE-based research directions for DLMs: we show that SAEs can provide useful signals for DLM decoding order; and the SAE features are stable during the post-training phase of DLMs. Our work establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows a great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.

papers.title: The Grammar-Learning Trajectories of Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: Do neural language models acquire linguistic phenomena in a consistent order during training, and what do their learning trajectories reveal about inductive biases?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models acquire grammatical phenomena in a consistent order across different initializations, architectures, and training data, suggesting a shared inductive bias, and their learning trajectory is approximately one-dimensional.
papers.conclusion: NLMs exhibit consistent learning trajectories, providing a valuable perspective for studying their inductive biases and linguistic representations, complementary to analyzing final model states.
papers.key_findings:
NLMs with different random initializations learn grammatical phenomena in a highly correlated order.
Different architectures (GPT2, TransformerXL) show similar learning trajectories when aligned by overall performance.
The choice of training data affects the learning trajectory but does not override the shared order; correlation increases with training.
The learning trajectory is essentially one-dimensional: models with similar overall performance have similar grammatical knowledge.
Early learning stages rely on local cues (e.g., bag-of-words), while later stages incorporate more context and structural information.
future_direction: Investigate the impact of additional factors, architectures, and learning phases that appear later in training.
papers.abstract: The learning trajectories of linguistic phenomena in humans provide insight into linguistic representation, beyond what can be gleaned from inspecting the behavior of an adult speaker. To apply a similar approach to analyze neural language models (NLM), it is first necessary to establish that different models are similar enough in the generalizations they make. In this paper, we show that NLMs with different initialization, architecture, and training data acquire linguistic phenomena in a similar order, despite their different end performance. These findings suggest that there is some mutual inductive bias that underlies these models' learning of linguistic phenomena. Taking inspiration from psycholinguistics, we argue that studying this inductive bias is an opportunity to study the linguistic representation implicit in NLMs. Leveraging these findings, we compare the relative performance on different phenomena at varying learning stages with simpler reference models. Results suggest that NLMs exhibit consistent "developmental" stages. Moreover, we find the learning trajectory to be approximately one-dimensional: given an NLM with a certain overall performance, it is possible to predict what linguistic generalizations it has already acquired. Initial analysis of these stages presents phenomena clusters (notably morphological ones), whose performance progresses in unison, suggesting a potential link between the generalizations behind them.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Large-Scale Counting in LLMs through a System-2 Strategy
papers.research_question: How can a test-time strategy inspired by System-2 cognitive processes overcome the architectural limitations of LLMs in large-scale counting tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a simple test-time strategy that decomposes large counting tasks into smaller sub-problems, enabling LLMs to surpass their architectural limitations and achieve high accuracy, and provides a mechanistic interpretation of how this System-2-like strategy functions within the models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed System-2 test-time strategy effectively overcomes the architectural limitations of LLMs in large-scale counting by decomposing the task, and mechanistic analysis reveals how count information is stored, transferred, and aggregated within the model.
papers.key_findings:
A System-2 strategy combining structured input (partitioning with a separator) and intermediate reasoning steps (Chain-of-Thought) enables LLMs to accurately count large numbers of items, overcoming the performance degradation seen in standard (System-1) counting.
Attention analysis shows that during intermediate reasoning, the model attends strongly to the final item/separator of each partition in middle-to-late layers (e.g., layers 19-23), and during final answer generation, it attends to the intermediate count tokens.
Causal mediation analysis (activation patching) identifies that count information is stored in the final item representations of each partition, transferred via specific attention heads, and aggregated to produce the final total.
The model's internal counting mechanism (System-1) is capacity-limited and degrades for counts beyond approximately 30 items due to transformer depth constraints, explaining the failure on large-scale counting.
Neither structured input alone nor Chain-of-Thought reasoning alone is sufficient for accurate large-scale counting; their combination is necessary.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on a narrow counting task with limited object diversity, using simple repeated nouns in synthetic contexts.
The approach depends on structured prompts and assumes prior knowledge of the model's reliable counting range, which may limit generalization.
The effects of tokenization and number representation are not isolated and may independently influence the results.
future_direction: Explore further applications of this strategy to complex reasoning tasks in language and beyond.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), despite strong performance on complex mathematical problems, exhibit systematic limitations in counting tasks. This issue arises from architectural limits of transformers, where counting is performed across layers, leading to degraded precision for larger counting problems due to depth constraints. To address this limitation, we propose a simple test-time strategy inspired by System-2 cognitive processes that decomposes large counting tasks into smaller, independent sub-problems that the model can reliably solve. We evaluate this approach using observational and causal mediation analyses to understand the underlying mechanism of this System-2-like strategy. Our mechanistic analysis identifies key components: latent counts are computed and stored in the final item representations of each part, transferred to intermediate steps via dedicated attention heads, and aggregated in the final stage to produce the total count. Experimental results demonstrate that this strategy enables LLMs to surpass architectural limitations and achieve high accuracy on large-scale counting tasks. This work provides mechanistic insight into System-2 counting in LLMs and presents a generalizable approach for improving and understanding their reasoning behavior.

papers.title: It Ain't That Bad: Understanding the Mysterious Performance Drop in OOD Generalization for Generative Transformer Models
papers.research_question: Why do generative transformer models exhibit strong in-distribution generalization but poor out-of-distribution generalization on arithmetic tasks, and is there a systematic pattern behind the OOD failures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that generative transformer models trained on n-digit arithmetic operations learn to map out-of-distribution inputs to outputs via equivalence classes modulo 10^n, explaining their poor OOD performance as systematic rather than random errors.
papers.conclusion: Generative transformer models exhibit equivalence generalization, mapping OOD inputs to ID equivalence classes, and representation learning plays a crucial role in both ID and OOD generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve near-perfect ID generalization but zero OOD accuracy on longer-digit arithmetic tasks.
The models learn an algebraic structure: they map OOD inputs to outputs by taking the operands modulo 10^n (for n-digit training), a phenomenon termed equivalence generalization.
Equivalence generalization is robust across different encoding methods, training data variations, and model scales.
Representation learning evolves from random to structured, enabling ID generalization but leading to systematic errors in OOD.
Increasing model size does not improve length generalization ability.
papers.limitation: The findings are based on synthetic arithmetic tasks and may not directly translate to natural language tasks due to the subjectivity and complexity of language.
future_direction: Using equivalence generalization as prior knowledge to guide training and reduce data needs
Applying equivalence class similarity metrics to domain adaptation for OOD generalization
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable proficiency on solving diverse problems. However, their generalization ability is not always satisfying and the generalization problem is common for generative transformer models in general. Researchers take basic mathematical tasks like n-digit addition or multiplication as important perspectives for investigating their generalization behaviors. It is observed that when training models on n-digit operations (e.g., additions) in which both input operands are n-digit in length, models generalize successfully on unseen n-digit inputs (in-distribution (ID) generalization), but fail miserably on longer, unseen cases (out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization). We bring this unexplained performance drop into attention and ask whether there is systematic OOD generalization. Towards understanding LLMs, we train various smaller language models which may share the same underlying mechanism. We discover that the strong ID generalization stems from structured representations, while behind the unsatisfying OOD performance, the models still exhibit clear learned algebraic structures. Specifically, these models map unseen OOD inputs to outputs with learned equivalence relations in the ID domain, which we call the equivalence generalization. These findings deepen our knowledge regarding the generalizability of generative models including LLMs, and provide insights into potential avenues for improvement.

papers.title: Synaptic state matching: a dynamical architecture for predictive internal representation and feature perception
papers.research_question: How can sensory cortex generate an internal simulation of the sensory environment in real-time? The paper investigates a neural architecture that oscillates between input-driven and recurrently-driven states to form predictive internal representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a neural architecture called Synaptic State Matching (SSM) that, through a local synaptic learning rule (Spike-Timing Dependent Covariance Plasticity), generates accurate and stable predictive internal representations of sensory input, enabling pattern completion and unsupervised feature detection.
papers.conclusion: Synaptic State Matching is a biologically plausible, parsimonious computational framework that unifies sequence learning, feature detection, synaptic homeostasis, and network oscillations to generate predictive internal representations, with potential applications in machine intelligence and time-series prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The SSM network can internally generate a perfect simulation of missing sensory input, acting as a short-term prediction.
SSM is remarkably robust to parameter variations, sensory noise, and structural perturbations like random synaptic ablation.
SSM networks can perform unsupervised feature detection and pattern completion from noisy input, forming receptive field maps reminiscent of biological visual cortex.
The learning process is stable and leads to a balance of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic drive into each neuron.
Multi-layer SSM networks can capture higher-order statistical regularities and perform dimensionality reduction.
future_direction: Search for molecular and cellular correlates of synaptic state matching.
Application of SSM networks in sequence learning, sequence generation, feature/object detection, time-series prediction, noise-filtering, and signal decomposition.
papers.abstract: Abstract Here we consider the possibility that a fundamental function of sensory cortex is the generation of an internal simulation of sensory environment in real-time. A logical elaboration of this idea leads to a dynamical neural architecture that oscillates between two fundamental network states, one driven by external input, and the other by recurrent synaptic drive in the absence of sensory input. Synaptic strength is modified by a proposed synaptic state matching (SSM) process that ensures equivalence of spike statistics between the two network states. Remarkably, SSM, operating locally at individual synapses, generates accurate and stable network-level predictive internal representations, enabling pattern completion and unsupervised feature detection from noisy sensory input. SSM is a biologically plausible substrate for learning and memory because it brings together sequence learning, feature detection, synaptic homeostasis, and network oscillations under a single parsimonious computational framework. Beyond its utility as a potential model of cortical computation, artificial networks based on this principle have remarkable capacity for internalizing dynamical systems, making them useful in a variety of application domains including time-series prediction and machine intelligence.

papers.title: Breaking Symmetry When Training Transformers
papers.research_question: How do Transformer architectures obtain positional information without positional encodings, and what is the role of causal attention and residual connections?
papers.core_contribution: Investigates the role of causal attention and residual connections in enabling Transformers to model positional information without positional encodings, finding that causal attention is necessary and residual connections aid convergence.
papers.conclusion: Causal attention is necessary for Transformers to model positional information without encodings; residual connections improve convergence but their role in preserving positional information is not definitively proven.
papers.key_findings:
Without causal attention, Transformer predictions are invariant to permutations of input tokens.
Causal attention is sufficient to break symmetry and enable modeling of input sequence order.
Residual connections are necessary for convergence when training Transformers without positional encodings.
Ablating too many residual connections prevents convergence on the three-digit addition task.
Correlation matrices suggest residual connections may help preserve positional information, but definitive evidence is lacking.
papers.limitation:
Experiments do not provide definitive evidence on whether residual connections help store positional information or merely help with convergence properties.
Negative convergence results might be due to insufficient hyperparameter tuning or training duration.
future_direction: Investigate the role of residual connections in preserving positional information while controlling for convergence effects.
papers.abstract: As we show in this paper, the prediction for output token $n+1$ of Transformer architectures without one of the mechanisms of positional encodings and causal attention is invariant to permutations of input tokens $1, 2, ..., n-1$. Usually, both mechanisms are employed and the symmetry with respect to the input tokens is broken. Recently, it has been shown that one can train Transformers without positional encodings. This must be enabled by the causal attention mechanism. In this paper, we elaborate on the argument that the causal connection mechanism must be responsible for the fact that Transformers are able to model input sequences where the order is important. Vertical "slices" of Transformers are all encouraged to represent the same location $k$ in the input sequence. We hypothesize that residual connections contribute to this phenomenon, and demonstrate evidence for this.

papers.title: Measuring Compositionality in Representation Learning
papers.research_question: How can we measure compositional structure in learned representations? And how does compositionality relate to learning dynamics, human judgments, representational similarity, and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Tree Reconstruction Error (TRE), a method for measuring compositional structure in learned representations, and applies it to study compositionality in relation to learning dynamics, human judgments, similarity, and generalization.
papers.conclusion: TRE provides a tool for evaluating compositionality in representation learning, opening up new directions for understanding models and the conditions that give rise to compositional representations.
papers.key_findings:
TRE tracks compositionality over learning, showing compression in the information bottleneck framework is associated with discovery of compositional representations.
TRE correlates with human judgments of compositionality for noun-noun compounds.
Compositionality (low TRE) imposes constraints on similarity between representations (Proposition 1).
In communication games, compositionality is correlated with generalization error, but low TRE is not necessary for good generalization and can sometimes indicate trivial strategies.
papers.limitation:
TRE requires oracle derivations (known compositional structure of inputs)
Low TRE can correspond to trivial strategies that yield poor overall performance
future_direction: Generalizing TRE to settings without oracle derivations (unsupervised grammar induction)
Using TRE to better understand existing machine learning models
Understanding data distributions and loss functions that give rise to compositional representations
papers.abstract: Many machine learning algorithms represent input data with vector embeddings or discrete codes. When inputs exhibit compositional structure (e.g. objects built from parts or procedures from subroutines), it is natural to ask whether this compositional structure is reflected in the the inputs' learned representations. While the assessment of compositionality in languages has received significant attention in linguistics and adjacent fields, the machine learning literature lacks general-purpose tools for producing graded measurements of compositional structure in more general (e.g. vector-valued) representation spaces. We describe a procedure for evaluating compositionality by measuring how well the true representation-producing model can be approximated by a model that explicitly composes a collection of inferred representational primitives. We use the procedure to provide formal and empirical characterizations of compositional structure in a variety of settings, exploring the relationship between compositionality and learning dynamics, human judgments, representational similarity, and generalization.

papers.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) solve arithmetic reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms or by memorizing training data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs solve arithmetic tasks by combining a sparse set of heuristic neurons, each implementing simple patterns, forming a 'bag of heuristics' rather than using a robust algorithm or memorization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arithmetic reasoning, rather than using robust algorithms or pure memorization.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse subset of MLP neurons in the arithmetic circuit implements simple heuristics for arithmetic.
Each heuristic neuron activates for specific input patterns and promotes corresponding answer tokens.
The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: Understanding In-Context Learning in Transformers and LLMs by Learning to Learn Discrete Functions
papers.research_question: What are the limits of in-context learning in Transformers, is attention necessary, can Transformers exploit teaching sequences for efficiency, and to what extent can LLMs implement learning algorithms from in-context examples?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformers can implement near-optimal learning algorithms for simple Boolean functions, struggle with complex ones like parities, and can adaptively use teaching sequences for sample efficiency. Additionally, pretrained LLMs demonstrate non-trivial in-context learning abilities on discrete tasks.
papers.conclusion: The study advances understanding of in-context learning in Transformers and LLMs, showing their capabilities and limitations on discrete function learning, and highlights the potential for adaptive algorithm selection.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers achieve near-perfect accuracy on simple Boolean functions like conjunctions and disjunctions.
Transformers fail to learn parity functions effectively, performing no better than random guessing.
Attention-free models such as Hyena perform similarly to Transformers on most tasks, with minor gaps on some.
Transformers can learn from teaching sequences and implement sample-efficient algorithms, adapting based on input.
Pretrained LLMs like GPT-4 and LLaMA-2 can compete with nearest-neighbor baselines on Boolean function tasks not in their training set.
papers.limitation: Transformers fail to learn parity functions effectively, performing no better than random guessing.
papers.abstract: In order to understand the in-context learning phenomenon, recent works have adopted a stylized experimental framework and demonstrated that Transformers can learn gradient-based learning algorithms for various classes of real-valued functions. However, the limitations of Transformers in implementing learning algorithms, and their ability to learn other forms of algorithms are not well understood. Additionally, the degree to which these capabilities are confined to attention-based models is unclear. Furthermore, it remains to be seen whether the insights derived from these stylized settings can be extrapolated to pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs). In this work, we take a step towards answering these questions by demonstrating the following: (a) On a test-bed with a variety of Boolean function classes, we find that Transformers can nearly match the optimal learning algorithm for 'simpler' tasks, while their performance deteriorates on more 'complex' tasks. Additionally, we find that certain attention-free models perform (almost) identically to Transformers on a range of tasks. (b) When provided a teaching sequence, i.e. a set of examples that uniquely identifies a function in a class, we show that Transformers learn more sample-efficiently. Interestingly, our results show that Transformers can learn to implement two distinct algorithms to solve a single task, and can adaptively select the more sample-efficient algorithm depending on the sequence of in-context examples. (c) Lastly, we show that extant LLMs, e.g. LLaMA-2, GPT-4, can compete with nearest-neighbor baselines on prediction tasks that are guaranteed to not be in their training set.

papers.title: Visual symbolic mechanisms: Emergent symbol processing in vision language models
papers.research_question: Do Vision Language Models (VLMs) employ emergent symbolic mechanisms, similar to those found in language models, to solve the binding problem for visual scenes? How do VLMs bind features to objects in multi-object scenes?
papers.core_contribution: This paper identifies a set of emergent symbolic mechanisms in VLMs that use content-independent spatial indices (position IDs) to bind visual features to objects, and demonstrates that binding errors in VLMs are directly caused by failures in these mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: VLMs employ emergent symbolic mechanisms for visual binding that use spatial position as a content-independent scaffold, and improving these mechanisms could reduce the binding failures that limit current VLM performance.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs employ a three-stage architecture with ID retrieval, ID selection, and feature retrieval attention heads that use position IDs (spatial indices) to bind features to objects.
Position IDs use a relative, rather than absolute, spatial coding scheme.
These symbolic mechanisms generalize beyond synthetic stimuli to complex, photorealistic images (PUG) and real-world images (COCO).
Position IDs are localized within the image patches corresponding to each object.
Binding errors in VLMs, such as in scenes with shared features (low entropy), are directly linked to failures in the position ID representation and can be mitigated by patching in robust position IDs from high-entropy scenes.
papers.limitation: The extent to which the identified mechanisms are truly emergent, and the role of architectural inductive biases (e.g., position embeddings) in driving their emergence, remains an open question.
future_direction: Investigate the role of architectural inductive biases in the emergence of visual symbolic mechanisms.
Improve binding performance via architectural innovations (e.g., object-centric architectures) or training strategies that strengthen symbolic mechanisms (e.g., spatial pointing tasks).
papers.abstract: To accurately process a visual scene, observers must bind features together to represent individual objects. This capacity is necessary, for instance, to distinguish an image containing a red square and a blue circle from an image containing a blue square and a red circle. Recent work has found that language models solve this 'binding problem' via a set of symbol-like, content-independent indices, but it is unclear whether similar mechanisms are employed by Vision Language Models (VLMs). This question is especially relevant, given the persistent failures of VLMs on tasks that require binding. Here, we identify a previously unknown set of emergent symbolic mechanisms that support binding specifically in VLMs, via a content-independent, spatial indexing scheme. Moreover, we find that binding errors, when they occur, can be traced directly to failures in these mechanisms. Taken together, these results shed light on the mechanisms that support symbol-like processing in VLMs, and suggest possible avenues for reducing the number of binding failures exhibited by these models.

papers.title: A Gray Box Interpretable Visual Debugging Approach for Deep Sequence Learning Model
papers.research_question: How can we visualize and debug the internal reasoning of deep learning models trained on audio sequence data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces d-DeVIS, a web-based interactive tool for visualizing and debugging deep sequence learning models by allowing users to manipulate audio inputs and observe layer-wise feature representations.
papers.conclusion: d-DeVIS allowed the users to visualize how CNN recognizes digits from audio sequence data and helped users develop a better intuition of the underlying reasoning of the model for more informed decisions in model development.
papers.key_findings:
d-DeVIS enables visualization of hidden layer features and weight distributions in CNN models for audio data.
The tool allows interactive manipulation of audio features to generate adversarial examples and observe model behavior changes.
It provides a gray-box debugging experience by making intermediate layer outputs transparent to users.
Users can compare different audio inputs and their extracted features to understand model decisions.
The system serves as a learning medium for academia and a platform for AI enthusiasts to experiment with deep learning models.
future_direction: Visualize other sequence deep learning models behavior and allow interactive manipulation of input data representation.
Visualize hidden layer complex feature representations for multi-modal sequence data.
papers.abstract: Deep Learning algorithms are often used as black box type learning and they are too complex to understand. The widespread usability of Deep Learning algorithms to solve various machine learning problems demands deep and transparent understanding of the internal representation as well as decision making. Moreover, the learning models, trained on sequential data, such as audio and video data, have intricate internal reasoning process due to their complex distribution of features. Thus, a visual simulator might be helpful to trace the internal decision making mechanisms in response to adversarial input data, and it would help to debug and design appropriate deep learning models. However, interpreting the internal reasoning of deep learning model is not well studied in the literature. In this work, we have developed a visual interactive web application, namely d-DeVIS, which helps to visualize the internal reasoning of the learning model which is trained on the audio data. The proposed system allows to perceive the behavior as well as to debug the model by interactively generating adversarial audio data point. The web application of d-DeVIS is available at ddevis.herokuapp.com.

papers.title: Interpreting and Improving Large Language Models in Arithmetic Calculation
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform arithmetic calculations, and can we improve their mathematical ability by fine-tuning specific components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that only a small fraction of attention heads and subsequent MLPs are responsible for arithmetic calculation in LLMs, and that selectively fine-tuning these components (Precise SFT) improves mathematical performance without degrading general abilities.
papers.conclusion: The study identifies sparse attention heads and MLPs for arithmetic calculation in LLMs and shows that precise tuning of these components improves mathematical capability with less impact on non-mathematical tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Only a small fraction (<5%) of attention heads are crucial for arithmetic calculation.
These heads attend to operands and operators.
Subsequent MLPs process the information to derive the answer.
The key components are transferable across datasets and tasks.
Precise fine-tuning of these components improves mathematical performance without harming general abilities.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily focus on LLaMA2 series, generalization to other LLMs needs further investigation.
The work focuses on arithmetic calculation, and more complex mathematical problems require further research.
future_direction: Generalize to a broader range of LLMs
Investigate more complex mathematical problems
Investigate shared and distinct mechanisms across mathematical tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential across numerous applications and have shown an emergent ability to tackle complex reasoning tasks, such as mathematical computations. However, even for the simplest arithmetic calculations, the intrinsic mechanisms behind LLMs remain mysterious, making it challenging to ensure reliability. In this work, we delve into uncovering a specific mechanism by which LLMs execute calculations. Through comprehensive experiments, we find that LLMs frequently involve a small fraction (< 5%) of attention heads, which play a pivotal role in focusing on operands and operators during calculation processes. Subsequently, the information from these operands is processed through multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), progressively leading to the final solution. These pivotal heads/MLPs, though identified on a specific dataset, exhibit transferability across different datasets and even distinct tasks. This insight prompted us to investigate the potential benefits of selectively fine-tuning these essential heads/MLPs to boost the LLMs' computational performance. We empirically find that such precise tuning can yield notable enhancements on mathematical prowess, without compromising the performance on non-mathematical tasks. Our work serves as a preliminary exploration into the arithmetic calculation abilities inherent in LLMs, laying a solid foundation to reveal more intricate mathematical tasks.

papers.title: Generalization or Memorization: Dynamic Decoding for Mode Steering
papers.research_question: How can we understand, identify, and control the distinct reasoning modes (generalization vs. memorization) in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Dynamic Mode Steering (DMS), a training-free inference-time algorithm that uses a linear probe and activation steering to dynamically steer LLMs from memorization to generalization, improving performance on reasoning and faithfulness tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a theoretical framework based on the Information Bottleneck to explain generalization and memorization, and introduces DMS, an inference-time control method that improves reasoning and factual accuracy by steering models towards generalization circuits.
papers.key_findings:
DMS significantly improves logical reasoning performance on GSM8K and commonsense reasoning on HellaSwag.
DMS reduces the generation of memorized falsehoods, improving factual accuracy on TruthfulQA.
The optimal intervention layer for DMS is identified via causal tracing, and performance degrades if applied at non-optimal layers.
The steering strength hyperparameter α has a concave relationship with performance, indicating a trade-off.
DMS outperforms strong baselines like greedy decoding, nucleus sampling, and contrastive decoding.
papers.limitation: Standard probing only reveals correlations and may detect features not causally used by the model.
future_direction: Development of unsupervised methods for discovering behavior vectors.
Extending DMS to multi-attribute control.
Further theoretical work to deepen the connection between the Information Bottleneck principle and the geometry of activation space.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit a troubling duality, capable of both remarkable generalization and brittle, verbatim memorization of their training data. This unpredictability undermines their reliability in high-stakes applications. In this work, we propose a unified framework to understand, identify, and control these distinct reasoning modes. First, we introduce a theoretical model based on the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle, formalizing generalization as the learning of a compressed, task-relevant representation and memorization as a failure to compress. Building on this theory, we develop Dynamic Mode Steering (DMS), a novel inference-time algorithm which comprises two components: (1) a lightweight, causally-grounded linear probe that identifies the model's instantaneous reliance on memorization, and (2) a dynamic activation steering mechanism that nudges the model's computation towards pre-identified generalization circuits. We frame DMS as a form of adaptive, self-contrastive decoding. Experiments on reasoning and faithfulness tasks demonstrate that DMS significantly improves logical consistency and factual accuracy, thereby offering a principled approach to enhancing LLM reliability.

papers.title: Probing for Arithmetic Errors in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can internal activations in language models be used to detect arithmetic errors?
papers.core_contribution: Simple probes can detect arithmetic errors from internal activations and enable lightweight self-correction via re-prompting.
papers.conclusion: Simple probes can extract predicted outputs and correct answers from internal activations, anticipate errors, generalize to chain-of-thought, and serve as weak oracles for self-correction.
papers.key_findings:
Probes can decode both the model's predicted output and the correct answer from hidden states with high accuracy.
Error detectors trained on these probes achieve over 90% accuracy in predicting model correctness.
Probes trained on simple arithmetic generalize to chain-of-thought reasoning on GSM8K problems.
Using error detectors to guide re-prompting corrects up to 11% of erroneous reasoning steps without degrading correct outputs.
Internal representations of numerical quantities are robust across contexts, enabling cross-setting generalization.
papers.limitation:
Focus on addition and subtraction, not other arithmetic operations like multiplication or division.
Experiments primarily on Gemma 2B IT, with limited evaluation on Phi-3.
Chain-of-thought analysis limited to addition-only GSM8K problems.
CoT evaluation uses structured equation formatting, not free-form natural language.
future_direction: Extend probing strategies to other arithmetic operations such as multiplication and division.
Broader evaluation across diverse architectures and model scales.
Explore other datasets with broader math coverage and varied reasoning formats.
Extend approach to operate over general, unstructured CoT traces.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether internal activations in language models can be used to detect arithmetic errors. Starting with a controlled setting of 3-digit addition, we show that simple probes can accurately decode both the model's predicted output and the correct answer from hidden states, regardless of whether the model's output is correct. Building on this, we train lightweight error detectors that predict model correctness with over 90% accuracy. We then extend our analysis to structured chain-of-thought traces on addition-only GSM8K problems and find that probes trained on simple arithmetic generalize well to this more complex setting, revealing consistent internal representations. Finally, we demonstrate that these probes can guide selective re-prompting of erroneous reasoning steps, improving task accuracy with minimal disruption to correct outputs. Our findings suggest that arithmetic errors can be anticipated from internal activations alone, and that simple probes offer a viable path toward lightweight model self-correction.

papers.title: Understanding Feature Selection and Feature Memorization in Recurrent Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How does a recurrent neural network (RNN) effectively detect and continuously extract relevant temporal structure from an input sequence, and how does it maintain the extracted feature in memory against incoming noise?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a fundamental conflict between feature selection and feature memorization in sequence learning with RNNs, and shows this conflict can be resolved either by using a gating mechanism (as in LSTM, GRU, PRU) or by increasing the state dimension (as in Vanilla RNN).
papers.conclusion: The F1B test reveals a fundamental conflict between feature selection and memorization in RNNs. Gating resolves this conflict dynamically, while Vanilla RNN requires increased state dimensions to separate the tasks across dimensions.
papers.key_findings:
Gated RNN models (LSTM, GRU, PRU) can pass the F1B test at state dimension 1 by dynamically adjusting their state-update equations.
Vanilla RNN fails the F1B test at state dimension 1 but passes at state dimension 2 by assigning different state dimensions to feature selection and memorization tasks.
The F1B test reveals the intrinsic capability of RNN models independent of any training algorithm.
There exists a conflict between the requirements for feature selection (amplifying the signal) and feature memorization (suppressing noise) in sequence learning.
Insights from the simplified F1B test are argued to be extrapolatable to more complex sequence learning settings.
papers.limitation: The F1B test is a simplified, synthetic setting and may not capture all complexities of real-world sequence learning tasks.
future_direction: Extending the test to a more general 'Flagged-k-Bit' test with multiple flags.
Developing new optimization techniques for Vanilla RNN to address gradient problems.
Exploring models that combine simpler gate structures with slightly increased state dimensions.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a test, called Flagged-1-Bit (F1B) test, to study the intrinsic capability of recurrent neural networks in sequence learning. Four different recurrent network models are studied both analytically and experimentally using this test. Our results suggest that in general there exists a conflict between feature selection and feature memorization in sequence learning. Such a conflict can be resolved either using a gating mechanism as in LSTM, or by increasing the state dimension as in Vanilla RNN. Gated models resolve this conflict by adaptively adjusting their state-update equations, whereas Vanilla RNN resolves this conflict by assigning different dimensions different tasks. Insights into feature selection and memorization in recurrent networks are given.

papers.title: Visualizing LLM Latent Space Geometry Through Dimensionality Reduction
papers.research_question: How does the internal geometric structure of latent states in Transformer-based language models evolve across layers and components?
papers.core_contribution: This paper visualizes and analyzes the latent space geometry of Transformer-based LLMs, revealing a clear geometric separation between attention and MLP component outputs, characterizing high-norm latent states at initial sequence positions, and visualizing layerwise evolution and positional effects.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates how dimensionality reduction can reveal geometric patterns in LLM latent spaces, contributing to interpretability research and motivating further analysis of feature geometry across models and conditions.
papers.key_findings:
A clear geometric separation exists between the outputs of attention and MLP components in intermediate layers, a pattern not previously documented.
Latent states at the initial sequence position have high norms, extending beyond special tokens in LLaMa despite its use of relative positional encodings.
Layerwise norms of latent states (excluding initial tokens) gradually increase and then spike in the final block before dropping after the final normalization.
GPT-2's learned positional embeddings form a high-dimensional helical structure in latent space.
LLaMa's sequence-position-dependent latent states show a low-dimensional geometric pattern, though the cause (RoPE vs. other factors) remains unclear.
papers.limitation: For LLaMa, the visualizations alone cannot determine whether the observed geometric patterns are due to RoPE, the convergence of features from self-attention heads, or both.
future_direction: Further understanding the dynamics of latent states across layers, models, and experimental conditions.
Interpreting the sequence-wise latent state geometric patterns of models using Rotary Positional Encodings (RoPE).
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve state-of-the-art results across many natural language tasks, but their internal mechanisms remain difficult to interpret. In this work, we extract, process, and visualize latent state geometries in Transformer-based language models through dimensionality reduction. We capture layerwise activations at multiple points within Transformer blocks and enable systematic analysis through Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP). We demonstrate experiments on GPT-2 and LLaMa models, where we uncover interesting geometric patterns in latent space. Notably, we identify a clear separation between attention and MLP component outputs across intermediate layers, a pattern not documented in prior work to our knowledge. We also characterize the high norm of latent states at the initial sequence position and visualize the layerwise evolution of latent states. Additionally, we demonstrate the high-dimensional helical structure of GPT-2's positional embeddings and the sequence-wise geometric patterns in LLaMa. We make our code available at https://github.com/Vainateya/Feature_Geometry_Visualization.

papers.title: Mechanistic Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: What are the primary mechanisms driving catastrophic forgetting in large language models during continual fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies three primary mechanisms of catastrophic forgetting in LLMs during sequential fine-tuning: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening around prior task minima.
papers.conclusion: Catastrophic forgetting in LLMs is driven by three interacting mechanisms (attention disruption, representational drift, loss landscape flattening), providing a mechanistic foundation for developing targeted continual learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 15-23% of attention heads, particularly in lower layers, undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, driving early forgetting.
Representational drift in intermediate layers, measured by CKA similarity, decreases by 0.32 to 0.47, indicating significant geometric changes.
Gradient interference, especially in query and key projection matrices, strongly predicts forgetting severity (correlation r=0.87).
The loss landscape around previous task minima flattens substantially (maximum Hessian eigenvalue drops from 147.3 to 34.2), making recovery difficult.
These three mechanisms interact and operate at different timescales, with attention disruption early, representational drift accumulating, and landscape flattening emerging later.
papers.limitation:
Experimental design focused on task sequences with clear boundaries, not continuous adaptation to gradually shifting distributions.
Examined forgetting over relatively short task sequences (4 to 6 tasks), while practical systems may encounter hundreds of sequential tasks.
Mechanistic analysis primarily characterized average behaviors across many model instances; understanding individual variability and rare failure modes remains important.
future_direction: Developing architecture modifications that inherently resist the identified forgetting mechanisms, such as attention heads with built-in stability constraints or intermediate layers with protected representational subspaces.
Designing optimization algorithms that explicitly manage gradient interference, representational drift, and landscape geometry during fine-tuning.
Creating diagnostic tools that monitor mechanistic signatures in real-time to prevent catastrophic forgetting before it occurs.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit remarkable performance across diverse tasks through pre-training and fine-tuning paradigms. However, continual fine-tuning on sequential tasks induces catastrophic forgetting, where newly acquired knowledge interferes with previously learned capabilities. Despite widespread observations of this phenomenon, the mechanistic understanding remains limited. Here, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of catastrophic forgetting in transformer-based LLMs during sequential fine-tuning. Through systematic experiments across multiple model scales (109B to 400B total parameters) and task sequences, we identify three primary mechanisms driving forgetting: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening. We demonstrate that forgetting severity correlates strongly with task similarity (Pearson r = 0.87) and gradient alignment metrics. Our analysis reveals that approximately 15 to 23 percent of attention heads undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, with lower layers showing greater susceptibility. These findings establish mechanistic foundations for developing targeted mitigation strategies in continual learning systems.

papers.title: Harmonic Loss Trains Interpretable AI Models
papers.research_question: Can harmonic loss, as an alternative to cross-entropy loss, improve interpretability, data efficiency, and reduce grokking in neural networks and LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces harmonic loss, an alternative to cross-entropy loss, which improves interpretability, data efficiency, and reduces grokking in neural networks and LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Introduces harmonic loss as an alternative to cross-entropy loss, finding that models trained with harmonic loss perform better by reducing grokking, requiring less data for generalization, and improving interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Harmonic loss leads to more interpretable representations (e.g., perfect circles in modular addition, lattice structures).
Harmonic loss reduces grokking (delayed generalization).
Harmonic loss improves data efficiency (requires less data to generalize).
Harmonic loss produces more interpretable weight vectors (e.g., class centers in MNIST).
Harmonic loss improves geometric structure in embeddings (e.g., better parallelograms in GPT-2).
papers.limitation: Scalability and applicability to even larger models need further study.
future_direction: Explore scalability and applicability to even larger models
papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce harmonic loss as an alternative supervisory signal for training neural networks and large language models (LLMs). Harmonic loss differs from standard cross-entropy loss by (a) replacing the usual SoftMax normalization with a scale-invariant HarMax function and (b) computing logits via Euclidean distance rather than a dot product. Harmonic loss enables improved interpretability and faster convergence, owing to its scale invariance and finite convergence point by design, which can be interpreted as a class center. We first validate the performance of harmonic models across algorithmic, vision, and language datasets. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that models trained with harmonic loss perform better than standard models by: (a) enhancing interpretability, (b) requiring less data for generalization, and (c) reducing grokking. Moreover, we compare a GPT-2 model trained with harmonic loss to the standard GPT-2, illustrating that the harmonic model develops more interpretable representations. Looking forward, we believe harmonic loss may become a valuable tool in domains with limited data availability or in high-stakes applications where interpretability and reliability are paramount, paving the way for more robust and efficient neural network models.

papers.title: Lost in Translation: The Algorithmic Gap Between LMs and the Brain
papers.research_question: What is the algorithmic gap between language models and the human brain, and how can we bridge it?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that despite computational-level equivalence in some tasks, language models diverge from human cognition at the algorithmic level, and proposes neuroscience-inspired architectural and training changes to bridge this gap.
papers.conclusion: The intelligence emerging from current LMs is fundamentally different from human cognition, and incorporating brain-inspired constraints may lead to AI with human-like flexibility and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Language models and the brain show representational similarities but likely use different algorithms.
Current LMs lack brain-like features such as sparsity, modularity, internal states, and interactive learning.
Incorporating brain-inspired features could lead to more human-like AI and better models of cognition.
future_direction: Incorporate sparse connectivity and modularity (e.g., MoE, RIMs) in LMs.
Add internal states and recurrence to transformers.
Develop continual and curriculum learning methods for LMs.
Ground LMs in embodied and social interactions.
Integrate oscillatory dynamics and scaling laws with efficiency constraints.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) have achieved impressive performance on various linguistic tasks, but their relationship to human language processing in the brain remains unclear. This paper examines the gaps and overlaps between LMs and the brain at different levels of analysis, emphasizing the importance of looking beyond input-output behavior to examine and compare the internal processes of these systems. We discuss how insights from neuroscience, such as sparsity, modularity, internal states, and interactive learning, can inform the development of more biologically plausible language models. Furthermore, we explore the role of scaling laws in bridging the gap between LMs and human cognition, highlighting the need for efficiency constraints analogous to those in biological systems. By developing LMs that more closely mimic brain function, we aim to advance both artificial intelligence and our understanding of human cognition.

papers.title: Probing the Difficulty Perception Mechanism of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether LLMs implicitly encode problem difficulty in their internal representations and how to locate the specific attention heads responsible for this perception.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLMs linearly encode problem difficulty in their internal representations and identifies specific attention heads responsible for this perception, providing a method for automatic difficulty annotation and revealing differences between difficulty perception and entropy.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that difficulty perception in LLMs is structurally organized and can be probed and localized, offering insights for adaptive reasoning and benchmark construction.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs linearly encode problem difficulty in high-dimensional embeddings, and a linear probe can accurately predict difficulty.
Specific attention heads in the final transformer layer show opposite activation patterns for simple and difficult problems.
Ablation experiments confirm the causal role of these attention heads in difficulty perception.
Difficulty perception at the token level does not consistently align with entropy variation.
Attention head patterns for difficulty perception can change with training, as seen in distilled models.
papers.limitation: whether the method based on attention head difficulty perception can be used for reward allocation in the RL training process.
future_direction: Investigating how pre-training and post-training quality affect difficulty perception.
Studying how attention head patterns change during training.
Exploring the relationship between token-level difficulty perception and entropy.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed on complex reasoning tasks, yet little is known about their ability to internally evaluate problem difficulty, which is an essential capability for adaptive reasoning and efficient resource allocation. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs implicitly encode problem difficulty in their internal representations. Using a linear probe on the final-token representations of LLMs, we demonstrate that the difficulty level of math problems can be linearly modeled. We further locate the specific attention heads of the final Transformer layer: these attention heads have opposite activation patterns for simple and difficult problems, thus achieving perception of difficulty. Our ablation experiments prove the accuracy of the location. Crucially, our experiments provide practical support for using LLMs as automatic difficulty annotators, potentially substantially reducing reliance on costly human labeling in benchmark construction and curriculum learning. We also uncover that there is a significant difference in entropy and difficulty perception at the token level. Our study reveals that difficulty perception in LLMs is not only present but also structurally organized, offering new theoretical insights and practical directions for future research. Our code is available at https://github.com/Aegis1863/Difficulty-Perception-of-LLMs.

papers.title: Echoes of BERT: Do Modern Language Models Rediscover the Classical NLP Pipeline?
papers.research_question: How do modern language models encode linguistic structure, and do they rediscover the classical NLP pipeline observed in earlier models like BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Modern language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline, with lexical information concentrated in early layers and becoming nonlinear, while inflectional morphology remains linearly accessible across layers and languages.
papers.conclusion: Modern transformer language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline and exhibit robust representational regularities for lexical and inflectional information across architectures, sizes, and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Modern LMs consistently organize linguistic information hierarchically: early layers process syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entities, later layers capture discourse.
Lexical identity (lemma) information is most accessible in early layers and becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network.
Inflectional morphology remains highly linearly accessible across all layers and across six typologically diverse languages.
These representational patterns emerge early during pretraining and are robust across model architectures, sizes, and training regimes.
Inflectional features occupy compact, linearly accessible subspaces in the residual stream, enabling effective steering interventions.
papers.limitation:
Representation extraction for decoder-only models uses the final subword token, which may not be optimal for all architectures.
The study does not explicitly examine cases where different grammatical functions share the same surface form (e.g., infinitive and non-past verb forms).
Classifiers only detect correlations in hidden activations, not causal mechanisms.
Steering experiments measure changes in classifier performance rather than downstream model outputs.
future_direction: Develop better extraction methods for word representations from decoder-only models.
Examine how models separate form from function across languages in cases of surface-form ambiguity.
Design more complex experiments to evaluate steering effects on actual model generation.
papers.abstract: Large transformer-based language models dominate modern NLP, yet our understanding of how they encode linguistic information relies primarily on studies of early models like BERT and GPT-2. Building on classic BERTology work, we analyze 25 models spanning from classical architectures (BERT, DeBERTa, GPT-2) to modern large language models (Pythia, OLMo-2, Gemma-2, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1), probing layer-by-layer representations across eight linguistic tasks in English. Consistent with earlier findings, we find that hierarchical organization persists in modern models: early layers capture syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entity-level information, and later layers encode discourse phenomena. We dive deeper, conducting an in-depth multilingual analysis of two specific linguistic properties - lexical identity and inflectional morphology - that help disentangle form from meaning. We find that lexical information concentrates linearly in early layers but becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network, while inflectional information remains linearly accessible throughout all layers. Additional analyses of attention mechanisms, steering vectors, and pretraining checkpoints reveal where this information resides within layers, how it can be functionally manipulated, and how representations evolve during pretraining. Taken together, our findings suggest that, even with substantial advances in LLM technologies, transformer models learn to organize linguistic information in similar ways, regardless of model architecture, size, or training regime, indicating that these properties are important for next token prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml5885/model_internal_sleuthing

papers.title: Beyond Human-Like Processing: Large Language Models Perform Equivalently on Forward and Backward Scientific Text
papers.research_question: Does the success of large language models arise from their flexibility as general pattern learners, rather than from human-like language processing mechanisms? This is investigated by training LLMs on forward and backward scientific text.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that transformer-based LLMs perform equally well on forward and backward scientific text, suggesting they are general pattern learning machines rather than models of human language processing.
papers.conclusion: Transformer-based language models are best understood as general pattern learning machines capable of extracting predictive structure from any sufficiently structured input, rather than as specific models of human language processing.
papers.key_findings:
Backward-trained GPT-2 models performed non-significantly better than forward-trained models on the BrainBench task.
Both forward and backward-trained models matched or exceeded human expert performance as model size increased.
Backward-trained models exhibited consistently higher perplexities on validation and test data.
Backward-trained models showed lower correlation with human judgments compared to forward-trained models.
Model judgments correlated more strongly with each other than with human judgments.
papers.abstract: The impressive performance of large language models (LLMs) has led to their consideration as models of human language processing. Instead, we suggest that the success of LLMs arises from the flexibility of the transformer learning architecture. To evaluate this conjecture, we trained LLMs on scientific texts that were either in a forward or backward format. Despite backward text being inconsistent with the structure of human languages, we found that LLMs performed equally well in either format on a neuroscience benchmark, eclipsing human expert performance for both forward and backward orders. Our results are consistent with the success of transformers across diverse domains, such as weather prediction and protein design. This widespread success is attributable to LLM's ability to extract predictive patterns from any sufficiently structured input. Given their generality, we suggest caution in interpreting LLM's success in linguistic tasks as evidence for human-like mechanisms.

papers.title: A mathematical theory of semantic development in deep neural networks
papers.research_question: What are the theoretical principles governing the ability of neural networks to acquire, organize, and deploy abstract knowledge by integrating across many individual experiences?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a mathematical theory of semantic development in deep linear networks, showing how hierarchical differentiation and other semantic phenomena emerge from the interaction of statistical structure and nonlinear learning dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The simple neural model qualitatively recapitulates many diverse regularities underlying semantic development, providing analytic insight into how statistical structure interacts with nonlinear deep learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Deep linear networks exhibit hierarchical differentiation of concepts through rapid developmental transitions.
The model accounts for semantic illusions during periods of developmental stasis.
Item typicality and category coherence emerge as factors controlling semantic processing speed.
Patterns of inductive projection change over development.
The similarity structure of internal representations is conserved across networks trained optimally.
papers.limitation: The linear model cannot capture complex nonlinear semantic phenomena such as context dependence, theory of mind, causal reasoning, and event structure binding.
future_direction: Theoretical analysis of more complex neural circuits to explain higher-level cognitive computations.
papers.abstract: An extensive body of empirical research has revealed remarkable regularities in the acquisition, organization, deployment, and neural representation of human semantic knowledge, thereby raising a fundamental conceptual question: What are the theoretical principles governing the ability of neural networks to acquire, organize, and deploy abstract knowledge by integrating across many individual experiences? We address this question by mathematically analyzing the nonlinear dynamics of learning in deep linear networks. We find exact solutions to this learning dynamics that yield a conceptual explanation for the prevalence of many disparate phenomena in semantic cognition, including the hierarchical differentiation of concepts through rapid developmental transitions, the ubiquity of semantic illusions between such transitions, the emergence of item typicality and category coherence as factors controlling the speed of semantic processing, changing patterns of inductive projection over development, and the conservation of semantic similarity in neural representations across species. Thus, surprisingly, our simple neural model qualitatively recapitulates many diverse regularities underlying semantic development, while providing analytic insight into how the statistical structure of an environment can interact with nonlinear deep-learning dynamics to give rise to these regularities.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

papers.title: Predicate learning in neural systems: Discovering latent generative structures
papers.research_question: How can latent representational structures (predicates) be learned from experience with unstructured data in neural systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper explains how predicate learning enables neural systems to discover latent generative structures from unstructured data using intersective comparison and neural oscillations, supporting compositionality and human-like generalization.
papers.conclusion: Predicate learning demonstrates how symbolic structures can be learned from neural signals, linking computational principles to neurophysiology and enabling complex human-like behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Predicate learning uses intersective comparison to detect invariants and form latent structures from unstructured data.
Neural oscillations, specifically desynchronization, enable dynamic binding of predicates and arguments without altering their meanings.
This approach allows for compositionality through rhythmic computation, facilitating the generation of new representations.
Predicate learning supports extrapolatory generalization to unseen data, as demonstrated in video game tasks.
It bridges symbolic representations and neural computation, offering insights into human cognitive processes.
papers.abstract: Humans learn complex latent structures from their environments (e.g., natural language, mathematics, music, social hierarchies). In cognitive science and cognitive neuroscience, models that infer higher-order structures from sensory or first-order representations have been proposed to account for the complexity and flexibility of human behavior. But how do the structures that these models invoke arise in neural systems in the first place? To answer this question, we explain how a system can learn latent representational structures (i.e., predicates) from experience with wholly unstructured data. During the process of predicate learning, an artificial neural network exploits the naturally occurring dynamic properties of distributed computing across neuronal assemblies in order to learn predicates, but also to combine them compositionally, two computational aspects which appear to be necessary for human behavior as per formal theories in multiple domains. We describe how predicates can be combined generatively using neural oscillations to achieve human-like extrapolation and compositionality in an artificial neural network. The ability to learn predicates from experience, to represent structures compositionally, and to extrapolate to unseen data offers an inroads to understanding and modeling the most complex human behaviors.

papers.title: The Other Mind: How Language Models Exhibit Human Temporal Cognition
papers.research_question: How do large language models exhibit human-like temporal cognition, specifically whether they spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point and adhere to the Weber-Fechner law?
papers.core_contribution: Larger LLMs spontaneously exhibit human-like temporal cognition, establishing a subjective reference point and adhering to the Weber-Fechner law, which emerges from multi-level convergence at neuronal, representational, and informational levels.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit human-like temporal cognition through multi-level convergence, suggesting cognition is a subjective construction of the external world. This points to the risk of alien cognitive frameworks and the need for AI alignment paradigms that guide internal world-building.
papers.key_findings:
In similarity judgment tasks, larger models spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point (ca. 2025) and their perception of time logarithmically compresses as years recede from this point, adhering to the Weber-Fechner law.
A subgroup of temporal-preferential neurons in the FFN exhibits minimal activation at the subjective reference point and implements a logarithmic coding scheme similar to biological systems.
Representations of years undergo hierarchical construction: from basic numerical values in shallow layers to abstract temporal orientation organized around a reference point in deep layers.
Pre-trained embedding models reveal that the training corpus possesses an inherent, non-linear temporal structure, providing raw material for the model's internal construction of temporal cognition.
The findings support an experientialist perspective where LLM cognition is a subjective construction of the external world by its internal representational system, leading to potential convergence with or divergence from human cognition.
future_direction: Evolve AI alignment beyond behavioral control to a paradigm that actively guides the formation of a model's internal world from its source.
Monitor models' emergent representational and cognitive patterns and enable intervention across the chain of cognition.
Curate the AI's environment with harmless or formalized verifiable information exposures.
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance, they exhibit certain cognitive patterns similar to those of humans that are not directly specified in training data. This study investigates this phenomenon by focusing on temporal cognition in LLMs. Leveraging the similarity judgment task, we find that larger models spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point and adhere to the Weber-Fechner law, whereby the perceived distance logarithmically compresses as years recede from this reference point. To uncover the mechanisms behind this behavior, we conducted multiple analyses across neuronal, representational, and informational levels. We first identify a set of temporal-preferential neurons and find that this group exhibits minimal activation at the subjective reference point and implements a logarithmic coding scheme convergently found in biological systems. Probing representations of years reveals a hierarchical construction process, where years evolve from basic numerical values in shallow layers to abstract temporal orientation in deep layers. Finally, using pre-trained embedding models, we found that the training corpus itself possesses an inherent, non-linear temporal structure, which provides the raw material for the model's internal construction. In discussion, we propose an experientialist perspective for understanding these findings, where the LLMs' cognition is viewed as a subjective construction of the external world by its internal representational system. This nuanced perspective implies the potential emergence of alien cognitive frameworks that humans cannot intuitively predict, pointing toward a direction for AI alignment that focuses on guiding internal constructions. Our code is available at https://TheOtherMind.github.io.

papers.title: Symmetry in language statistics shapes the geometry of model representations
papers.research_question: Why do geometric structures (circles, loops, manifolds) arise in the internal representations of language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that translation symmetry in pairwise co-occurrence statistics of natural language explains the emergence of geometric structures (e.g., circles, manifolds) in the internal representations of language models.
papers.conclusion: Representational manifolds have a universal origin: symmetry in the statistics of natural data.
papers.key_findings:
Empirical observation of representation manifolds (circles, loops) and linear coordinate decoding in shallow word embedding models like word2vec.
